corr.detail: The source gives: One primary stress per word at the right edge: a word whose final syllable is closed is stressed on that final syllable; a word whose final syllable is open is stressed on the penult, regardless of the length of the final vowel. Because word-final short vowels were lost or lengthened very early, most words end in a stressed closed syllable, so surface stress is predominantly final. The author holds these rules constant 'throughout most of the history of Aramaic' (Proto-Aramaic through the Middle Aramaic period that sec. 1.2.3 defines as Palmyrene, Hatran, Nabatean and Qumran Aramaic), with retraction to the penult only in some Late Aramaic dialects.

Phrasal recordings were examined briefly for some classes of words where it was thought that phrasal stress may have been interfering with a p…

2694.heavy: Heavy syllables are those which contain a long vowel or a coda consonant (Barkhouse 1998); light syllables contain a short vowel. Heavy syllables will be considered to be bimoraic (regardless of how many moraic elements they may have, as in the case of (C)VːC or (C)VCC syllables, for example), while light syllables will be considered monomoraic.
2694.dflt: All-light word: feet built right-to-left over light syllables, the initial syllable always stressed (degenerate foot), primary on the rightmost stress. In isolation the word-final short vowel behaves as heavy (bimoraic) and takes primary stress: [(ma_u)('la_uu)] 'home', [('ku_uu)] 'island', [('po_uu)] 'on one side' (p. 277 ex. 13a, Olson writes the final vowel as a short vowel carrying two moras, not as a long vowel). Phrase-medially the final short vowel is unstressed and the 3-syllable all-light words in ex. 13b surface with one initial stress after clash deletion ([('me)ni.ku], [('a)na.po]); penult primary for longer all-light words (e.g. (LL)('LL)) follows from rule (10) but no such example is given in the paper.
2694.prule: Quantity-sensitive: moraic (bimoraic) trochees built right-to-left, degenerate feet allowed; every heavy syllable (long vowel or coda consonant) is stressed, the initial syllable is stressed, every second light syllable counting from the right is stressed; primary stress = the rightmost stressed syllable (End Rule Right). In practice primary stress is on a heavy final syllable; a word-final short vowel counts as heavy (bimoraic) and takes primary stress in isolation/citation forms but not phrase-medially, where the primary falls on the rightmost surviving foot head to its left. Olson's only phrase-medial examples of all-light words (3 syllables, ex. 13b p. 277) surface with a single initial stress after clash deletion: [('me)ni.ku] 'island', [('a)na.po] 'on one side'; the penult stress that rule (10) would predict for them is removed by clash resolution.
2694.srule: Every stressed syllable other than the rightmost (primary) one bears secondary stress: every heavy syllable (long vowel or coda consonant), the word-initial syllable, and every second light syllable counting right-to-left within a run of light syllables (e.g. [ˌnaqaˌniːˈket], [ˌeˌlipqaˌmuːˈtoq]). Optional clash resolution among light syllables only: the rightmost stress of a clash may be deleted (mostly in connected speech) or, in isolation, the word-initial member strengthened; all-heavy words are exempt.

2694.tone: Not a tone language. 2695.quote: Prosody (tone and stress) Although it seems that Milang is most likely a tone language, unfortunately I have been unable to analyse the tone system of Milang up to date. Work on tone in Milang is difficult because even native speakers are not aware of the tones, and sometimes realize them in different ways. This is similar to what Post (2015b) describes for Eastern Tani languages. Similarly for stress. I hope that in the future it will be possible to analyse the prosody system of Milang.

2696.prule: Lexical tone: three level tones (low, mid, high) plus two contours (low-high, high-low), inventory explicitly provisional; tone is contrastive on monosyllables (minimal pairs given). No word-stress or accent rule is stated anywhere in the description.
2696.quote: The language has been recorded with three tone levels: à low, ā mid, á high. In addition, two contour tones have been observed: ǎ low-high, â high-low. While the number of contrastive tones cannot be considered as definitive, there is no doubt that Gali is a tone language, as is a priori expected for any Chadic language. Illustrative minimal pairs are: nǝ̀ “we” ≠ nǝ́ “I”; pààṛ “blood” ≠ pááṛ “sun”; tǝ̀ṛ “man” ≠ tǝ́ṛ “moon”.

2697.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (penult), quantity-insensitive; stated as a tendency ('tends to be', 'appears to go') with many unexplained exceptions.

2698.prule: Lexical tone language (Douglas: seven tones, 'chiun-pian, e-pian, chiun-sian, chiun-khi, e-khi, chiun-jip, e-jip', with pervasive tone sandhi). No word-stress rule: prominence is a group-level 'accent' on the tone-sandhi group of 2-4+ monosyllabic words. Primary accent falls on the last word of the group, which alone keeps its citation tone; non-final words change tone; enclitic words (marked by a double hyphen) are unaccented and lose their tone, so the primary accent then sits on the penult or antepenult of the group. In a group of three: primary on the last, secondary on the first, middle unaccented (with listed exceptions where the first is an auxiliary/function word or the second has a stronger tone). Group of four = two groups of two, each accented on its second word.
2698.srule: Douglas 1873 states group-internal secondary accent: two-word group without hyphen (subject + verb, hong chhe) = secondary + primary, the first word keeping its tone; hyphenated compound (hong-chhe) = unaccented + primary. Three-word group: secondary on the first word, middle unaccented (2-0-1); secondary shifts to the second word (0-2-1) when the first is an auxiliary/function word (u, bo, eng, lai, khi, beh, prepositions, tsap, chit...) or the second has a much stronger tone, unless the first is specially important. Four-word group = two groups of two, each accented on its second word, the first sub-group weaker (0-2-0-1; the secondary 'often almost as strong as the primary'); with tsap or a weak word in second place 3-0-2-1 with a tertiary accent on the first. Groups of five or more are compounded of shorter groups likewise. The last of two enclitics may carry a faint secondary accent without recovering its tone.

tn.quote: In Amoy, though nominally there are eight, yet really there are only seven, as the second tone class, the "chiūⁿ-siaⁿ," is not divided into two. ... The two jip tones, or the upper and lower fourth tone, stand quite by themselves. They are distinguished by being pronounced with an abrupt or clipped ending ... The other five tones are distributed among the words which do not end in h, k, p, or t. Two of these five tones are perfectly level, just like musical notes ... The three tones which remain are more or less inflected, and cannot be represented by any musical notes.

2703.heavy: Not weight: the stress-attracting property is tone. A syllable bearing tone 1 (high) or tone 2 (mid) that immediately precedes a tone-3 (low) syllable attracts loudness/stress ('may be louder than the first syllable'); otherwise the first syllable of the couplet. Couplet-initial vowel lengthening (blocked before a glottal stop) is a fixed correlate of the couplet, not a conditioning weight.
2703.dflt: First syllable of the couplet (root-initial): 'Loudness, stress, usually occurs on the first syllable of the couplet.'
2703.prule: Explicit word-stress statement inside a three-tone system (tones 1 high, 2 mid, 3 low; tone clusters such as 1-3, 2-3). Stress is equated with loudness and placed by a tone-conditioned rule with a couplet-initial default: 'Loudness, stress, usually occurs on the first syllable of the couplet' (the couplet = the bimoraic root, the minimal phonological word; prefixes lie outside it), 'When, however, tone 1 or tone 2 precedes tone 3, the syllable preceding the tone 3 may be louder than the first syllable' (villu1-yu3 'my (polite) cat', ei3so2-yu3 'my (polite) brother-in-law': the couplet's second syllable, before the tone-3 enclitic -yu3, is louder), the loudness being 'especially noticeable' on the tone clusters 1-3 and 2-3 (villu1-3, ei3so2-3). Independently of tone, the couplet-initial vowel is lengthened unless it precedes a glottal stop. No weight- or syllable-count conditioning: position is set by the tone string over the couplet plus post-couplet material, so the record goes to the house bucket for tone-driven stress used for the sister Mixtec systems in this run (ayut1236, caca1250).

2704.prule: Stress is bound to lexical roots: every (monosyllabic) root is stressed; in a root=root compound the stress falls on the last syllable, i.e. the second root (Tabla 89: giS=ˈtil 'pan', Zob=ˈze 'maíz', Zob=ˈStil 'trigo', gig=ˈbe' 'río'); a word-final vowel enclitic (/+i/ 'allí', /+a/ 3INAN) is never stressed, so root+clitic words are stressed on the root (first syllable: /ˈbiep+i/, /ˈbdob+a/), while phonologically eroded second-position roots (/ie/ < /nie/ 'verde', /ie'n/ 'pequeño') do take stress because they are lexical roots. Position is thus set by morpheme class (root vs clitic), not by syllable count or weight.

2704.tone: Tonal language: five tones, of which four are lexically contrastive (alto, bajo, bajo ascendente, alto ascendente) and one is a derived falling tone (tono derivado, descendente) used only on the second syllable of two-root compounds (2007 ch. 4, pp. 96, 111-112; 2015 ch. 4 with sandhi). Stress is treated separately as 'acento de intensidad' (2007 sec. 5.4), non-contrastive ('no hay contraste entre átonas y tónicas en raíces monosilábicas'); vowel enclitics are unstressed, short and always high-toned. The 2015 doctoral thesis never uses 'acento' (0 hits for acento/acentu in the whole text); it recasts the same facts in moraic/foot terms: root+clitic = trochaic foot (heavy-light) with the clitic outside the phonological word (p. 185: 'El clítico vocálico que se le agrega a estas palabras es de una mora y queda siempre fuera de la palabra fonológica formando así un grupo clítico'; foot-type summary p. 186; sec. 3.4.4 pp. 196 and 198: 'este clítico queda fuera de la palabra fonológica', 'el clítico queda fuera de la palabra fonológica'); root=root compound = iambic foot, first root reduced to one mora (pp. 185-187; sec. 3.4.5 pp. 198-199).

2705.heavy: Primary position quantity-insensitive. Raum: a long vowel ('ein langer Vokal') before the tonic syllable carries 'eine Art Nebenton' (secondary accent); a monosyllable with a long final vowel (ndžā, mō, mī, -kā, -fē) 'hält aber den Ton fest, so daß sie nicht enklitisch werden können' (p. 36).
2705.prule: Raum 1909 §6: word accent ('Betonung', 'Ton', 'Tonsilbe') ordinarily rests on the penultimate syllable, stated as the general Bantu rule ('Die Grundregel für die Betonung im Bantu') and applied to Mochi with Mochi examples (ndžĕkápa, wŏlóka, walĕhénda, hénda-ṅu, ṅgakúnda-se-fo'); quantity-insensitive; hedged 'Gewöhnlich' and at once qualified: Mochi tends ('Tendenz') to de-accent derivational suffixes in favour of the stem syllable, giving stem-initial (antepenultimate) accent in causatives (wávĭṛa, -sahĭṛa, osáhĭṛo, -támŭṛa); a monosyllabic word encliticises to a polysyllabic host and the host's accent moves to its last syllable (kapa-mbe), except the genitive particle; adverbial enclitic suffixes do not move the verb's accented syllable. Pitch ('Intonation', three tones) is treated separately in §7. Modern sources give no positional stress rule: Nurse & Philippson 1977 analyse Old Moshi as a two-tone (H/L) language and say nothing about stress; Philippson 1991 describes Chaga (Vunjo data, Mochi included via Winter 1987) as combining a fully distinctive tone system with a demarcative accent that is lexically placed on the penult or the final of the stem (or absent) and realised only at the end of a prosodic group; Winter 1987 (excerpt) posits three distinctive 'prosodemes' each bundling a Druckakzent with a pitch interval, DPI/DPII assigned lexically to the first stem syllable. The old positional statement and the modern lexical-accent-plus-tone analyses cannot be reduced to one rule.
2705.srule: Raum 1909 §6: 'a kind of secondary accent' (eine Art Nebenton) falls on a long vowel that stands before the tonic (penultimate) syllable, e.g. walĕhénda 'that they will not go', ndžĕkápa 'I shall strike', wŏlóka 'they climb down'; no other non-primary stresses are described. tn.quote: Die Hauptbedeutung der Intonation im Motschi ist die, daß sie das Mittel ist, sonst gleichlautende Wörter zu unterscheiden. Als solches spielt sie eine wichtige Rolle und ist sorgfältig zu beobachten. Es scheint mir, daß es nötig ist, im Motschi drei Töne, einen Hochton, Zeichen [raised barred stroke], einen Mittelton, Zeichen [raised stroke] und einen Tiefton, Zeichen [lowered stroke] zu unterscheiden. tn.translation: The chief significance of intonation in Mochi is that it is the means of distinguishing otherwise identical words. As such it plays an important role and must be carefully observed. contra.head: The published descriptions contradict each other
contra.detail: Two reachable primaries give irreconcilable positions for polysyllabic words: Eloranta 2020 adopts Hovdhaugen's initial/root-syllable stress; Cerrón-Palomino 1995 argues automatic penultimate stress throughout cap. VI, then prints 'antepenúltima' in the concluding sentence. 2708.prule: Primary stress falls on the last vowel (last syllable) of the dictionary citation form, i.e. the stem without inflectional endings. Prefixes (e.g. possessive/person m-, ny-, etc., described pp. 307-313) precede it; all endings (the nominalizer -ve 'the place that', the tense/switch-reference and other endings of 'Mojave Words in Sentences') are never accented, and the accent does not move when endings are added. In citation forms, Tone 1 is realized with a high pitch in the first half of the rime, usually with a falling contour [˦˨] in nonchecked syllables. In contrast, Tone 2 is characterized by a mid-level pitch in the first half of the rime, often accompanied by a rise toward the end [˨˧].' 'Moklen can thus be considered a language with word tones, as each prosodic word can only bear one tone on the stressed syllables. The initial syllables of disyllables are always phonologically toneless. Quantitatively speaking, the tonal contrast is marginal as few minimal pairs exist.' 2717.dq: In elk woord treft men een klankgreep (soms twee) aan, waarop we meer drukken dan op de andere, en die we dan ook met krachtiger ademdruk uitspreken. In het lonkundó valt het intensiteitsaccent gewoonlijk op de eerste klankgreep van den stam.
2717.prule: Dynamic (intensity) accent on the first syllable of the stem (root-initial), whatever the number of prefix syllables; a monosyllabic stem without suffix throws the accent onto the prefix, with a suffix it keeps it on the stem. Position is read off the prefix-stem-suffix parse, not off syllable count or weight.
2717.srule: Hulstaert 1938 gives no placement for a second stress: a word has one stressed syllable, 'soms twee' (sometimes two). Placement per Boelaert 1952 (verse prosody, offered as provisional): polysyllabic words often carry two dynamic accents, the 'accent racique' on the first syllable of the stem and the 'accent mécanique' on the penultimate syllable of the word or on certain infixes; either may be the principal accent, the other the weaker; dynamic accents never fall on adjacent positions.

2717.tone: Two-tone language (Sect. V 'Toonshoogte', pp. 9-10: 'Er bestaan twee enkelvoudige tonen: de hooge (á) en de lage (a)', with rising/falling contours from combinations). Author separates dynamic accent from tone explicitly: 'het intensiteitsaccent gaat niet noodzakelijkerwijze met een hoogeren muzikalen toon gepaard... Beide taalelementen: intensiteitsaccent (kracht) en muzikaal of tonisch accent (toonshoogte), moeten steeds goed uit elkaar gehouden worden', and says stress is 'lang niet zoo belangrijk als de toonshoogte'. Boelaert 1952: no constant relation between tone and dynamic accent. Since a positional stress rule is stated alongside the tone system, tone or pitch accent is not the right code; the tone facts are carried here.

tn.quote: Elke klankgreep wordt op een bepaalde toonshoogte uitgesproken. ... Er bestaan twee enkelvoudige tonen: de hooge (4) en de lage (a). In deze spraakkunst zijn onbetoonde klankgrepen te beschouwen als laag. Verbindingen dezer tonen geven een stijgenden toon (a) en een dalenden toon (4). In samentrekkingen en elisies komen nog voor: de svijgend-dalende toon (4) en de dalend-stijgende toon (a), alsook, doch zelden, een vierdubbele toon, de dubbelstijgende toon (a). Men dient elk woord aan te leeren met zijn eigen toon.
tn.translation: Every syllable is pronounced on a definite pitch. ... There are two simple tones: the high (a with acute) and the low (a). In this grammar unmarked syllables are to be taken as low. Combinations of these tones give a rising tone and a falling tone. In contractions and elisions there further occur the rising-falling tone and the falling-rising tone, and also, though rarely, a quadruple tone, the double-rising tone. One must learn each word with its own tone.
tn.cite: Hulstaert, G. 1938. Praktische grammatica van het Lonkundo (Lomongo) (Belgisch Kongo). (Kongo-Overzee Bibliotheek.) Antwerpen: De Sikkel.
tn.locator: Inleiding, Sect. V 'Toonshoogte (muzikaal of tonisch accent)', p. 10
tn.note: Two level tones, high (á) vs low (unmarked); rising/falling are combinations of these, rise-fall and fall-rise only in contractions/elisions. Each vowel of a diphthong has its own tone.

2718.prule: No word-stress rule is stated and none is recoverable: the language is extinct (corpus of 19th-c. wordlists) and no source gives precise suprasegmental information. APS 23 p. 244 (saved JSTOR text, scan-noisy): 'Accent is of the utmost importance in both these dialects, and the identity to the eye of various words as nyujmi, ear and smoke, arises from absence of proper accent marks in my authorities.... Unfortunately, none of my authorities employ any accentual mark but the acute, and this appears to be syllabic.' (the nolō/nolô 'snake/flower' pair is Albornoz's Chiapanec, applied to Mangue by analogy). Posiblemente, y porque otras lenguas de la familia los poseen, el mangue tuvo tono y cantidad.'

2719.dq: All possible combinations of level tones occur in monosyllabic, bisyllabic and trisyllabic words. [Tone is illustrated at word level on citation forms and in a read passage; no stress or prominence of any domain is described.]

2719.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Mono is described as a three-level tone language (H, M, L; rising and falling tones analysed as sequences of level tones) with lexical tone (minimal triplet áwá/āwā/àwà) and grammatical tone (verb TAM, H-L-H melody on locative adverbs, polarity on prefix /ga-/). The words stress, accent and prominence do not occur anywhere in the six-page article; the transcribed passage carries tone marks and pause bars only.

2719.idn: Describes the Mono variety spoken in Bili, Bosobolo Zone, DRC (the prestige variety per Olson 2004: 233; 'the Bili dialect' in Paster 2006).
2719.tone: Three level tones H /´/, M /¯/, L /`/ (áwá 'diarrhea', āwā 'road', àwà 'fear'); contours = sequences of level tones; all level-tone combinations occur in 1-3 syllable words; grammatical tone: tone on the first syllable of the verb root depends on tense, aspect and mood, the infinitive takes prefix /kə́-/ plus L on the first root syllable (p. 234); H-L-H melody on certain locative adverbs; tonal polarity on prepositional prefix /ga-/. Nothing at all is said about stress or accent (neither asserted nor denied). Length and nasalization are not contrastive (p. 235).
